title: Transition Metals and Coordination Compounds

cards.b: Ruby red, emerald green, blue copper sulphate, rust brown: transition metals give us colour. They also run catalysts that make fertiliser, carry oxygen in your blood (iron in haemoglobin) and power batteries and magnets.
They occupy the d-block (Groups 3-12), such as Ti, Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu, Zn. Their atoms are filling d orbitals. They are typically hard, dense, high-melting and good conductors.

• Variable oxidation states: iron is Fe2+ or Fe3+; manganese goes from +2 to +7.
  • Coloured compounds: d electrons absorb part of visible light; we see the rest.
  • Catalysts: Fe in Haber, V2O5 in sulphuric acid, Ni in hydrogenation of oils, Pt in converters.
  • Form complex ions.

In a complex, ligands split the d orbitals into two energy levels. An electron absorbs a specific colour of light to jump up. The compound shows the complementary colour. Copper(II) sulphate solution absorbs orange-red, so looks blue.

Zn2+ and Sc3+ have empty or full d subshells, so no jumps, and their compounds are colourless.

Alfred Werner (1893) proposed that a central metal ion binds a fixed number of molecules or ions called ligands, through dative bonds (both electrons come from the ligand). He won the 1913 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

The number of ligand bonds is the coordination number. Six usually gives an octahedral shape; four gives tetrahedral or square planar.

• Haemoglobin: Fe2+ in a ring (haem) carries O2.
  • Chlorophyll: Mg2+ complex, the green photosynthesis pigment.
  • Vitamin B12: cobalt complex.
  • Cisplatin: square-planar platinum complex, a cancer drug (approved 1978).
  • EDTA: grips metal ions, used to treat lead poisoning and soften water.

In K4[Fe(CN)6], potassium is +1 (4 of them = +4) and each cyanide is -1 (6 = -6). Sum is zero: 4 + x - 6 = 0, so x = +2. Fe is +2.

Charge on [Cu(NH3)4]2+: ammonia is neutral, copper is +2, so the complex ion is 2+. Coordination number = 4.

• Zinc is not typically a transition metal as its d shell is full in all its compounds.
  • A ligand does not need a charge. Water and ammonia are neutral ligands.
  • Colour is not only from the metal. Changing ligands changes the colour.
  • Catalysts are not magic. They offer an alternative reaction path through changing oxidation states.

Ruby is aluminium oxide with a trace of chromium (Cr3+), giving a red colour; emerald (beryl) is coloured by chromium too, while blue sapphire owes its hue to iron and titanium. India's gem industry, with Jaipur for coloured stones and Surat for cutting and polishing diamonds, relies on such transition-metal chemistry to grade, treat and sell stones.

• Transition metals: variable oxidation states, colour, catalysis, complex ions.
  • Werner (1893): metal centre plus ligands; coordination number often 6.
  • Biology uses them: Fe in haemoglobin, Mg in chlorophyll, Co in B12.
